name: Balor

facts.text: Level 81, 40,000 health, Tur Suil's final; he takes 30% less from slash, crush and thrust.
At every tenth of health lost (90% down to 10%) he spawns an Eye of Balor: a flying, untargetable eye that casts Balor's Eye Light, heat damage.
He cannot be hurt outside his tether and calls nearby kin into the fight.
Allakhazam lists him as a level-81 humanoid in Tur Suil, without description.
Irish myth: Fomorian king with a destroying eye, killed by Lugh at the second battle of Mag Tuired.
Muirgen, Eochaidh of Ardee, Fiachna of Howth, Gleann Glas and the seven hides are Living Server lore.
In Irish myth Lugh slew Balor at the second battle of Mag Tuired with a sling-stone through the eye.

story:
In the realm's myth Balor was king of the Fomorians, whose eye, poisoned by his father's druids' cauldron, destroyed whatever it saw; he shut his daughter Eithne in a tower on Tory against a prophecy, and her son Lugh drove the eye out through his skull at the second battle of Mag Tuired, where it fell facing the Fomorian host and destroyed it.

The Sylvan of Domnann know a second verse: the eye's bearers, who always walked backwards, wrapped it in seven hides and carried it west; the Fomorians themselves say the eye followed its people of its own will. When the hides slipped on the shore of Hy Brasil it looked on a valley for one breath and burned the Sylvan village of Gleann Glas and everything else in it; that is the Vale of Balor. On the crag above, the Fomorians built Tur Suil, the tower of the eye, with one window, and grew a king around the eye again, with a household: Sargan and Norsob, Kierac and the Master of Pain, Abomos, Queen Qunilaria, and the Balorians.

Eochaidh of Ardee's three groups learned his fight and died at the eighth eye: his hide turns blades, he cannot bleed outside his chamber, and every tenth of his strength lost opens another unreachable eye that burns whoever it sees. Fiachna of Howth's small raid brought him down the next spring, carrying a smooth stone for Lugh's sake, and every Tur Suil raid has carried one since. He returns, the Vale glows red more often, Qunilaria's diggers may be near the Root, and the Fomorians wait for the lid to rise fully. Muirgen, who set all this down in 'The Tower of the Eye', ended it with a warning from the old tale: towers do not hold everything, and the realm must keep climbing.
legend: Blades bite him less than spells do, so casters carry this fight. Every tenth of his health another eye opens over the room and burns someone; you cannot target them, so spread out and heal through the light. Fight him in his chamber and kill the adds he calls. Never meet his eye, the old hibs say, and they do not mean it as a joke. Casters carry it, melee holds, everyone spreads. Count his tenths aloud so the healers know when the next eye opens, and never chase him if he drifts toward the door. Old hibs end every briefing the same way: never meet his eye.

loremasterTopic.text: The eye's memory of a king, grown back in Tur Suil. Steel bites him poorly. Each tenth of his strength lost opens another eye in the room, and each eye burns. Spread out and do not meet his gaze.

bookPage: A Sylvan who carried water for the raid that killed him told Muirgen what she saw. The king did not look at anyone. He did not need to. Each time the warriors cut him deeper, something opened in the dark under the roof: an eye, red at the rim, and wherever it looked a person burned. She counted nine. When he fell they all closed together, she said, like a house putting out its lamps. She does not believe they are gone. She believes they are waiting, as the eye waited in its seven hides on the long voyage west, for someone to let the hides slip.

chapters.title: The King of the Fomorians
chapters.text:
Every Hibernian child learns the tale, and the bards of Tir na Nog sing it the same way they have for an age. Balor was king of the Fomorians, the sea-people of the old days who held these coasts before the Tuatha came. As a boy he crept to the door of a hall where his father's druids were brewing a spell, and the fumes of the cauldron rose into one of his eyes, and from that day the eye destroyed whatever it looked upon. He kept it shut under a lid so heavy that four men had to raise it with a polished handle, and on the battlefield they raised it toward the enemy, and the enemy died. The bards add that the Fomorians who marched behind him could never let him turn round.

A druid foretold that Balor would die by the hand of his own grandson. He had one child, a daughter named Eithne, and he shut her in a tower on Tory, the rock of the northern sea, so that no man should ever reach her. A man reached her anyway, as the bards say men always do, and she bore a son. Balor had the infant thrown into the sea; the child was saved, and raised far away among the Tuatha, and his name was Lugh.

These things are the realm's myth, older than any record, and Muirgen, the druid of Tir na Nog who went to Hy Brasil with the first of the realm's swords and wrote 'The Tower of the Eye', took care to say so. What follows in this telling is what the Sylvan of Hy Brasil told her, and what the realm has learned since, in the tower itself.

chapters.title: Mag Tuired, and the Second Verse
chapters.text:
At the second battle of Mag Tuired the Tuatha and the Fomorians met for the last time, and Balor's bearers raised the lid. Lugh, who had come to the battle against all advice, put a stone in his sling and drove it through the eye so hard that the eye went out through the back of Balor's skull, and fell, still open, facing the Fomorian host behind him. Its gaze killed his own army. That is where the Hibernian bards end the song, and that is why the Fomorians lost the old war and went into the sea.

The Sylvan of Domnann know a second verse. They say the Fomorians who lived through Mag Tuired were the eye's own bearers, the men whose duty had always been to walk backwards before their king so that his gaze would never fall on them, and that when the eye fell they were the only ones not looking at it. They wrapped it, still open, in seven hides of seven beasts, and carried it to the shore without once turning round, and put to sea. The Sylvan say the Fomorians still keep the names of the seven beasts and will tell no outsider what they were.

There is a third account, from the Fomorians themselves, as the Sylvan have overheard it in the shore stair of Fomor. In that telling Balor did not die at Mag Tuired at all, only lost his eye for a while, and the eye was not carried but followed its people west of its own will, looking for them. The Sylvan think this is the Fomorians comforting themselves. Muirgen thought it was the most frightening of the three.

chapters.title: The Vale of Ash
chapters.text:
The boat came to Hy Brasil in a mist, as all boats come there, in the age when the isle was still hidden and the Sylvan believed no one could find it. The Fomorians found it because they were not looking for it, the Sylvan say; Hy Brasil hides from those who search. They came ashore on the eastern coast, below a crag above a green valley, and as they carried the eye up the beach the hides slipped.

The eye looked at the valley for as long as it takes to draw breath. Everything in its gaze died: the trees, the grass, a Sylvan village called Gleann Glas whose name the Sylvan still say at their fires, and every creature in the valley down to the worms. The bearers covered it again. The valley has never grown back. The Sylvan call it by Balor's name now, the Vale of Balor, and walk round it rather than through, and the realm's scouts who cross it report that the ash there is still fine and grey under the grass that has crept in at its edges, and that nothing lives in the middle of it at all.

The Sylvan date the Fomorians' coming to Hy Brasil from that day, and the beginning of the long encroachment that Hibernia's first allies on the isle asked the realm to help them stop. When the Sylvan came down to the shore to ask the realm for swords, the Vale was the first thing they named, before Fomor and before the Root.

chapters.title: The Tower with One Window
chapters.text:
On the crag above the burned valley the Fomorians built a tower to hold the eye. They built it as Balor in the old tale built a tower on Tory to hold his daughter: tall, with one window, so that whatever was kept inside could see out and nothing could come in. They named it Tur Suil, which Muirgen glossed as the tower of the eye, and set the eye behind the window, and began, slowly, over long generations, to grow a king around it again.

How, nobody outside the tower knows. The Sylvan believe the Fomorians fed the eye, as the hydrars of Fomor feed their hydra, and that a body grew from what it was fed; they point to the Sylvan raiders whose spirits Abomos the Soultrapper keeps in his cells, and say the king was built from such things. The druids of Tir na Nog believe the eye built the body itself, out of its memory of the king who once carried it, and that the Balor of Tur Suil is the eye's idea of a king rather than a king. Muirgen's note in the margin of her book takes the druids' side: the eye was never his; he was always the eye's.

Around the king the Fomorians set a household. Sargan the Conqueror and Norsob the Annihilator to hold the western halls, kept apart because they hate each other. Kierac the Destroyer to guard the torturer's hall, with the Master of Pain living inside him. Abomos to keep the cells. Queen Qunilaria to dig. And soldiers, the Balorians, named for the heroes the Fomorians had killed.

chapters.title: Nine Wounds, Nine Eyes
chapters.text:
The Balor of Tur Suil is huge and slow, and his hide turns a third of every blade: the realm's warriors learned early that steel bites him poorly and that spells carry this fight. He is bound to his chamber at the top of the crag, and beyond it the tower will not let him bleed. He calls his kin from the halls when he is pressed. None of that is why the realm fears him.

The eye in his face is shut now, its lid a slab of flesh nobody has ever seen raised. But it is not the only eye in Tur Suil. The first band of the realm to reach his chamber, a force of three groups led by a champion of Ardee named Eochaidh in the first winter of the isles, found out what happens when he is wounded. Every time his strength fell by a tenth, another eye opened in the dark under the roof of his chamber, high up, beyond any sword, red at the rim, and wherever it looked a person burned with the same light that had ash-blackened the Vale. No ward stopped it; no blade could reach it. Nine wounds, nine eyes. Eochaidh's band counted them, and Eochaidh's band died at the eighth.

The survivors' lesson is the one every Hibernian raid now follows. Spread out, so that no eye finds two fighters at once; count his tenths aloud, so the menders know when the next eye opens; and heal through the light rather than trying to escape it. The bards say Balor's gaze killed his own army at Mag Tuired. In his tower, they say, it has learned to be selective.

chapters.title: Lugh's Stone
chapters.text:
The first raid to bring him down came in the next spring, and the realm's records remember that it was small: two groups and a third for the stair, under a bard of Howth named Fiachna who had studied every account of Eochaidh's band. Fiachna carried a smooth stone in his pack all the way up the tower, for Lugh's sake, and the raiders laughed at him for it. He told Muirgen afterwards that he had never needed it and had been glad of it the whole way.

When Balor fell, all the eyes in his chamber closed together, like a house putting out its lamps. Muirgen's Sylvan water-carrier, who had gone up with the raid, did not believe they were gone; she believed they were waiting. The king returns, as the eye does, and the realm goes up the tower again whenever the Vale glows red at night, which is the sign the Sylvan of the eastern coast watch for.

Every Hibernian raid to Tur Suil since has carried a smooth stone. It is the realm's oldest raid custom on Hy Brasil, older than the four doors of Sheeroe, and the raiders who laugh at it are told Fiachna's story. Nobody has ever thrown one. The bards say that is as it should be: the stone was Lugh's to throw, and the realm only carries it to remind the eye who its grandson was. Fiachna's own stone lies on the sill of the one window of the king's chamber, where he set it on the way down; no Fomorian has ever moved it.

chapters.title: What the Eye Wants
chapters.text:
The Sylvan believe the eye wants to see everything, and that this is all it has ever wanted: an eye that was put out once wants nothing so much as to look. Balor sits in his chamber and looks out of the one window over the isle, and his household works for him. Queen Qunilaria's brood digs downward under the crag, and in recent seasons, the Sylvan report, it broke into something soft and very old far below that smells of sap. They believe the eye's diggers are close to the roots of Olcasgean, the Root of Galladoria, and that nobody has ever thought what happens when the eye in the tower and the Root in the hollow meet.

The Fomorians of Fomor have their own hope, which the Sylvan have overheard in the shore stair: that one day the lid will rise fully, and on that day the city will climb the stair together and take the isle, and then the sea, and then the land beyond the sea that they lost at Mag Tuired. The druids of Tir na Nog take it seriously. They have noted that the Vale glows red more often than it did in the first seasons, and that the Fomorian raids on Domnann follow the glow by a few weeks.

In the old tale the prophecy said Balor would die by his grandson, and he shut his daughter in a tower, and it did not help. Muirgen ended her book with that: towers do not hold everything. The realm keeps climbing this one, every generation, to make sure.
